hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about what kind of radiation is able to pass through the body but is absorbed by different amounts in bone, muscle and other tissues.
Hint 2: Think about the limitation of a normal X-ray photograph where all the overlapping structures are squashed onto one flat image.
Hint 3: Consider how looking at just one thin slice at a time, rather than the whole body at once, would give much clearer detail.
Hint 4: Think about how the X-ray tube and detectors could be moved around the patient to view that same slice from lots of different directions.
Hint 5: Think about what a powerful computer could do with hundreds of slice images taken along the body to show the inside in three dimensions.
parts.proper_answer: X-rays are used. A narrow collimated beam scans a thin section or slice of the object. The tube and detectors rotate so many scans of each section are taken at different angles. The transmitted intensity gives the attenuation for each path. A computer processes the data to form a 2D image of the section. Images of many adjacent sections are combined to form a 3D image.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Start With X-rays and Attenuation**
Think of CT as a much smarter X-ray. I am sending a narrow beam of X-rays through you. Different tissues attenuate the beam by different amounts, following $$I = I_{0}e^{-\mu x}$$ where $\mu$ is the attenuation coefficient. Bone with high $\mu$ absorbs a lot, soft tissue absorbs less. Detectors on the opposite side measure the transmitted intensity $I$.

Step 2: **Scan Thin Slices, Not the Whole Body**
A normal X-ray puts everything on top of each other in one flat shadow. In CT I only look at one thin slice or section at a time. The beam is collimated to that slice, so I get sharp detail with no overlap from structures above or below.

Step 3: **Rotate Around to See From Many Angles**
One view of a slice is not enough. I rotate the X-ray tube and the detectors around the patient, typically through 360 degrees. That way I take hundreds of scans of the same slice from many different angles, building up a complete map of attenuation in that plane.

Step 4: **Let the Computer Build the Image**
Now I hand all those intensity readings to a computer. It solves for the attenuation of each tiny volume element and converts it to shades of grey to make a detailed 2D cross-sectional image of that slice. Then I move along the body and repeat for many adjacent slices.

Step 5: **Stack Slices Into 3D**
Finally I stack all those 2D slice images together in the computer. Because I have slice-by-slice detail through the whole region, I can reconstruct a full 3-dimensional view of internal organs, bones and tumours that can be rotated and viewed from any direction.
